content.title: Response
content.comment:
We thank the reviewer for the valuable comments and concerns. To our understanding, the main points are (1) concerns that our comparisons are not fair for some experiments (Figures 5, 6, 7) (2) the generality of our findings (3) hyperparameters sensitivity. We address them below.

> In my opinion, the comparison is not fair for many experiments. For example, the x-axis represents steps in Figure 5, 6, 7. That means the number of epochs is increased for the same number of steps when you scale up the batch size. When the agent can be trained with more data, the convergence will be faster. So I think the s-axis should be the number of epochs.

In line with the SAC-N paper, we fix one epoch to 1k gradient updates, so the number of epochs is actually equal in all the comparisons (Figures 5, 6, 7, and 8 in the updated paper). However, it is true that with larger batches agent sees a lot more training data for the same number of training steps, although it does not make comparisons unfair as we are interested in scaling properties of different batch sizes in these experiments. As data is static (unlike in online RL) we are not limited by sample efficiency bottleneck and can study scaling properties increasing only our limit for GPU computing. 

At the end, the most important is relative wall-clock training time and not the amount of offline data that the agent absorbed during the training (as long as the dataset is the same for all methods), this may be of interest in some works, but we believe this is an orthogonal issue. In Table 9 and Figures 3, 11 , we demonstrate that the relative training time until convergence for larger batches is indeed a lot shorter. Thus, we believe that these experiments are fair.

> To verify the generality of your proposed method, maybe you can provide more experimental results about other methods.

As we answered the similar concern of the reviewer ****D2xN****, in our work, we specifically focused on Q-ensemble methods as these methods significantly outperform non-ensemble predecessors on a large portion of the D4RL benchmark, and their convergence times are highly extended when compared to non-ensemble methods (this is demonstrated in Section 3 for both SAC-N and EDAC methods), therefore making experimentation longer.

And in general, we purposefully do not claim that scaling batch size will work on other algorithms, as this is not true even in supervised learning. Where LARS [1] will work, LAMB [2] may not, and otherwise. Nevertheless, it is certainly an intriguing direction for future work, as we state in Appendix A.2 in the updated paper. 

> Sensitivity analysis about hyper-parameters, such as learning rate. We know RL is more sensitive to hyper-parameters.

Indeed, RL is famously known to be very sensitive to hyper-parameters and we share this concern with the reviewer. However, all important hyperparameters not relevant to our work were taken from previous works since it is known that they work well on all D4RL and are robust. As for our paper, we use a single value for learning rate and batch size across all 18 datasets and show that LB-SAC achieves speedups on almost all of them, 4x on average, without tuning batch size and learning rate. We believe this is enough to show that our hyperparameters are sufficiently generic and robust.

Additionally, we provide ablations on the learning rate (Section 6.2) showing that just increasing the learning rate is not enough.

___
*References*

1. You, Y., Gitman, I., & Ginsburg, B. (2017). Large batch training of convolutional networks. *arXiv preprint arXiv:1708.03888*.
2. You, Y., Li, J., Reddi, S., Hseu, J., Kumar, S., Bhojanapalli, S., ... & Hsieh, C. J. (2019). Large batch optimization for deep learning: Training bert in 76 minutes. *arXiv preprint arXiv:1904.00962*.

content.title: Response
content.comment:
We thank the reviewer for the valuable comments. According to the review, the main concerns are (1) lack of formal introduction to the SAC-N and EDAC methods and underlying mechanism of conservatism and (2) lack of clear motivation for why our paper is valuable for the community. We address them below.

> SAC-N algorithm is not formally desribed before being mentioned in the introduction. I cannot find a reference for SAC-N after reading the entire paper.

Thank you for pointing out the missing explanation of the SAC-N algorithm. We agree, that there should be a more detailed description in the paper that relies on it and its modifications. To correct this, in the updated version of the paper we include a new section fully devoted to the SAC-N explanation and mechanism of conservatism that emerges from the usage of an ensemble for value estimation (Section 2).

> However, it seems a straightforward adoption of well-known large-scale deep learning training methods. Could the authors explain why this study is needed and why it's not obvious that previously established fast training methods may not work in the offline RL setting?

While we are not aware of any results and studies examining or using large batches in offline RL (and only a few works in the online RL [1, 2, 3]) it is indeed true, that there is a large body of work on large batch optimisation in supervised deep learning. 

However, in supervised learning, it is well known that most of the proposed methods for large batch optimisation do not generalize well to different architectures or fields [4] (or even hurt generalization in general [5, 6]). That is the case and motivation for the two most popular adaptive optimizers: LARS [7] and LAMB [8]. LARS is known to work well only for CNN and CV tasks while harming performance for MLP’s and Attention-based architectures. LAMB on the other hand works better for Transformers but needs hyperparameter tuning in practice, as well as learning rate warmup. Thus, it is not an obvious fact beforehand that such techniques can be transferred to the Offline RL methods and will work. Moreover, hyperparameter tuning can be limited in offline RL setting.

In the paper, we also showed that for SAC-N, adaptive optimizers do not provide any benefits (Ablations, Section 6.3), thus pointing to possible future research directions.

> I'm not convinced that this paper solves a problem unique to offline RL or generates any novel insights on how to better design efficient offline RL methods.

In our experience, unlike modern NLP or CV, in offline RL, most methods (even those that use ensembles) utilize modern GPU's (V/A 100) at only 10-15% which leaves a lot of room for scaling.   Additionally, for ensembles, it is typical to train for longer than 2-3 hours, while we can reduce this time by a factor of 4 and get 100% utilization.

It seems lucid to us that if we can train methods faster, we should do so since it will speed up experimentation and shorten the feedback loop, and that's what the online RL community is also dedicated to [9, 10, 11, 12]. However, judging from the new and concurrent papers based on Q-ensembles for offline RL (to which our findings may apply), the increase in batch size is not common wisdom and not obvious to the researchers. For instance, BURL [13], RORL [14], and MSG [15] all use a batch size of 256 and don’t mention any batch size specific tuning or comparison.

Thus, we think that our findings are novel to the offline RL community and can be useful for a growing number of works on Q-ensembles.

content.confidence: 4: You are confident in your assessment, but not absolutely certain. It is unlikely, but not impossible, that you did not understand some parts of the submission or that you are unfamiliar with some pieces of related work.
content.summary_of_the_paper: The authors investigate the effect of large batch size in training the SAC algorithm. The result shows that a large batch size allows the algorithm to converge faster and introduces a form of conservatism (shown through the standard deviation ratio between ID vs. OOD state/action). This effect cannot be achieved by layer-wise optimization or learning rate alone.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength:
The overall quality of the paper is high. The paper is well-written, and there are some ablation experiments to support the main argument of the paper.

Weakness:
My main criticism of this paper, which ultimately led me to a borderline reject decision, is that this paper treats RL as if it were supervised learning. If I replace SAC with ResNet in every part of this paper, and D4RL with ImageNet or CIFAR-10, only section 4.2.1 (Bigger Batch Size Penalize OOD Actions) would not make sense, but all the rest would still be fine. For example, 4.2.2 (batch size ablation), 4.2.3. (learning rate), 4.3 (a better optimizer) all offer no explanation from the RL perspective.

Section 4.2.1 offers an explanation of why the large batch size would help, and it says:
> One possible explanation for why earlier penalization might be helpful is for prevention of the iterative error exploitation (which is prominent in iterative algorithms and extensively discussed in Brandfonbrener et al. (2021)), as it allows to soften the overestimation bias early in the training process making its propagation less severe.

In the TD3/SAC algorithm, critics are updated using the bellman-backup operator:

$$L = \mathbb{E}\_{\tau \sim D}[(r\_{t+1} + \gamma \min_j Q_{\theta_j}(s_{t+1}, \tilde a + \epsilon) - Q_{\theta_i}(s_t, a_t))^2]$$

This is a moving target, which is influenced by how well the Q-function is trained.
One can argue, with larger batch size, bellman value propagation is more random at the start -- because you essentially fit $r$ with a random noise outputted by an untrained Q function. So it's possible that large batch size helps reduce the "early commitment" issue.
Therefore, a simple experiment to understand why large batch size helps is to just add Gaussian noise to the critics' target during early training and anneal this noise to see if you can recreate this effect of large batch size.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
Clarity: The paper is very clear. Figures and tables are well-explained, and effects well-explained.
Novelty: the direction of large batch size's effect on RL is relatively novel and under-investigated.
Reproducibility: the reviewer is fairly confident that the result can be reproduced.
Quality: The overall writing quality is high.
content.summary_of_the_review: The paper shows that large batch size empirically helps with conservatism but offers no explanation of why this phenomenon occurs, and how it impacts the RL algorithm (except for some simple statistics that are used to describe the phenomenon). All the observations/experiments are superficial. If the authors fail to offer more significant insight and cannot design an experiment that reveals why larger batch size leads to more conservatism, this paper does not offer enough contribution to the research community.
content.correctness: 4: All of the claims and statements are well-supported and correct.

content.title: Response
content.comment:
Thank you for the feedback. According to the review, the main concern is an insufficient explanation for the observed result, and therefore an absence of valuable insight. We address it below.

> Therefore, a simple experiment to understand why large batch size helps is to just add Gaussian noise to the critics' target during early training and anneal this noise to see if you can recreate this effect of large batch size.
> 

Thank you for the proposed experiment, we run it and observed that the use of annealed gaussian noise does not help to converge faster achieving commensurate times with the original SAC-N algorithm. This made us to reconsider the original conjecture on the softened overestimation bias and moved us to a simpler yet effective explanation, which we outline below.

> If the authors fail to offer more significant insight and cannot design an experiment that reveals why larger batch size leads to more conservatism, this paper does not offer enough contribution to the research community.
> 

In the updated version of the paper, we added more analysis on the observed effect (Section 5.2). Essentially, the explanation is conceptually simple, yet valuable: additional experiments show that if one is keeping the original SAC-N algorithm for more training steps (10 million instead of typically employed 1 million), *the std ratio still keeps growing* (for in-dataset actions it stays on the same level, but for OOD actions it continues to increase)*.* The use of large batches allows us to achieve the same levels way faster in the training process (see Figure 6). This essentially means that the lower number of critics can already provide a sufficient level of diversity, but needs to be trained for longer, and ultimately, the use of large batches helps to do it significantly quicker.

> If I replace SAC with ResNet in every part of this paper, and D4RL with ImageNet or CIFAR-10, only section 4.2.1 (Bigger Batch Size Penalize OOD Actions) would not make sense, but all the rest would still be fine. For example, 4.2.2 (batch size ablation), 4.2.3. (learning rate), 4.3 (a better optimizer) all offer no explanation from the RL perspective.
> 

We agree that these experiments may not offer much explanation from the RL perspective, yet, we believe they help the reader to isolate the effects and demonstrate that the use of established LBO optimizers can be avoided in favor of a simpler method.

display_title: Response, Issue #1: On Limited Applicability and Impact

content.title: Response, Issue #1: On Limited Applicability and Impact
content.comment:
> This paper only focuses on SAC-N and doesn't study any other offline methods. Thus this work is tightly coupled to a very specific method and it is hard to draw general conclusions from these results.

In our work, we specifically focused on Q-ensemble methods due to several reasons. First, these methods significantly outperform non-ensemble predecessors on a large portion of the D4RL benchmark [1, 2, 3,  4]. Second, their convergence times are highly extended when compared to non-ensemble methods (this is demonstrated in Section 3 for both SAC-N and EDAC methods), therefore making experimentation longer.

As the development and use of the ensemble-based methods are getting attention in the offline-RL community [2, 3, 4], we believe our findings are valuable, since we described a simple yet effective approach that can increase the level of penalization provided by the ensemble without (1) an additional optimization term and (2) additional hyperparameters (e.g. EDAC requires careful tuning of the eta parameter). Moreover, we conceive our results are important as they highlight that a smaller number of critics can already provide a sufficient level of diversity for datasets considered (without explicitly making them so) but just needs to be trained for longer to attain a similar level of penalization (and we showed that it can be avoided with larger batches, see Section 5.2). 

In this case, if the main issue was the reliance on the soft-actor critic algorithm as the backbone, we are not aware of competitive offline-RL model-free q-ensemble methods that use a different backbone (one could point to the REM method [5], but it heavily underperforms SAC-N). Moreover, note that the original EDAC paper also studied its diversification effect based on the SAC algorithm only. If we are missing some relevant literature, we are certainly open to adding more experiments.

___
*References*

[1] An, G., Moon, S., Kim, J. H., & Song, H. O. (2021). Uncertainty-based offline reinforcement learning with diversified q-ensemble. *Advances in neural information processing systems*, *34*, 7436-7447.

[2] Ghasemipour, S. K. S., Gu, S. S., & Nachum, O. (2022). Why So Pessimistic? Estimating Uncertainties for Offline RL through Ensembles, and Why Their Independence Matters. *arXiv preprint arXiv:2205.13703*.

[3] In Review at ICLR2023, “Lightweight Uncertainty for Offline Reinforcement Learning via Bayesian Posterior”, [https://openreview.net/forum?id=55Eet8WGJTv](https://openreview.net/forum?id=55Eet8WGJTv)

[4] Yang, R., Bai, C., Ma, X., Wang, Z., Zhang, C., & Han, L. (2022). RORL: Robust Offline Reinforcement Learning via Conservative Smoothing. *arXiv preprint arXiv:2206.02829*

[5] Agarwal, Rishabh, Dale Schuurmans, and Mohammad Norouzi. "An optimistic perspective on offline reinforcement learning." *International Conference on Machine Learning*
. PMLR, 2020.

display_title: Response, Issue #2: On the Experimental Setup

content.title: Response, Issue #2: On the Experimental Setup
content.comment:
> The definition of convergence time seems arbitrary to me. This is an important issue as the main claim of this paper is improving training time based on the "convergence" time. I understand that this paper follows [2] to define this metric. But the setting of this paper seems different from them as [2] works with a large language model and having a metric like that might make sense [?].

We chose this definition of convergence time as it summarizes the actual training duration until a certain level of performance is achieved. This is important as it highlights that making one iteration faster does not necessarily mean your algorithm will converge faster. We extensively discuss this in the Section 3, arguing that this approach is more fair since it accounts for another dimension — an algorithm may take longer for one training step but require way less such steps, which is the case for LB-SAC.

To further illustrate our point, we also added convergence times for different levels of performance in the appendix (Figure 13). One can see, that the large batches are also favorable under these conditions as well.

In case the issue is the particular choice of +/- value, we derived it as a standard deviation typical for this class of algorithms.

> This paper only considers a small subset of D4RL tasks which doesn't help the paper either.

In the updated version of the paper, we added more datasets (all datasets for Walker2D, HalfCheetah, and Hopper) — now it’s 18 datasets as opposed to the initial 9. The statements we made in the original version of the paper apply to those datasets as well, moreover, LB-SAC outperforms both EDAC and SAC-N on average (86.4 vs 85.2 vs 84.5).

> Also, halfcheetah, walker2d, and hopper all have very small state and action spaces whereas environments like FrankaKitchen and Adroit in D4RL have larger state and action space. Hence increasing batch sizes like in MuJoCo experiment might not be possible in those other environments as the network can't fit in a single gpu.

To demonstrate that the use of large batches does not present an overwhelming memory overhead for agents operating with proprioceptive states, we run an additional experiment comparing SAC-N, EDAC, and LB-SAC on the Ant environment: 119 combined dimensions for both the state and action spaces (for reference, Adroit has 69 combined dimensions). The comparison table can be found in the appendix (Table 5), to summarize:

LB-SAC: score=126, training time=21 minutes, memory=3.2gb, num critics=10

EDAC: score=116, training time=72 minutes, memory=2.85gb, num critics=10

SAC-N: score=121, training time=116 minutes, memory=2.47gb, num critics=50

We believe this amount is modest enough, as it will still fit into modern and not-that-modern GPUs (e.g., GeForce GTX 980 Ti, 2015 year of release, allows for 6Gbs of memory)**.** 

Important to note is that the main reason for memory amplification is the ensemble size. For example, if one goes for an image-based environment like CARLA, a 10k batch for one network is quite modest. For instance, for the Carla dataset, it would take around 250mb of memory. However, this value then should be multiplied by the number of ensemble members. But, as we demonstrated in the paper, larger batches actually reduce the required ensemble size.

However, you’re still correct that the large batches might need more memory, and in some cases would not be suitable. On the other hand, if one is operating with even higher-dimensional problems, they can use data-parallel pipelines (e.g. with Accelerate).

display_title: Response, Issue #3: Performance relative to EDAC

content.title: Response, Issue #3: Performance relative to EDAC
content.comment:
> EDAC results are better in both terms of training time and final results than SAC-N. Also it has better memory consumption per table 2 results in this paper. Thus I am not sure why one should still consider SAC-N.

You’re correct that the EDAC results are better in terms of the training time than the original SAC-N algorithm. However, in our work, we argued for the proposed large-batch optimization approach (which we denote in our paper as LB-SAC), and it outperforms both EDAC and SAC-N in terms of the convergence time — 3-4x on average (please, see the updated version of the paper, as the OpenReview does not allow to edit the abstract).

As for the normalized scores, in the first version of the paper, we relied on exactly the same number of critics as in the EDAC paper for almost all of the datasets. In the updated version, we did a sweep across a different number of critics and updated the resulting scores. Now, we outperform both SAC-N and EDAC in terms of the resulting performance on the whole locomotion suit (see Table 4), and match EDAC scores on the initial datasets considered (see Table 1). Moreover, we could make the necessary number of critics even smaller, and convergence time faster: from 60 minutes on average to 40-50 minutes.

In our work, we were not aiming to argue in favor of the original SAC-N algorithm, but rather the proposed modification with the batch size increase.

As for memory consumption, indeed, there is a trade-off that we wanted to demonstrate. However, the resulting sizes for typically employed offline-RL datasets are far from the limits of the modern (and not that modern) GPUs, which we discussed [below](https://openreview.net/forum?id=V5NFgHyNBI8&noteId=7I5VvjWN2U).

display_title: Response, Issue #4: On Novelty and Impact

content.title: Response, Issue #4: On Novelty and Impact
content.comment:
We are not aware of any results and studies examining large batches in offline RL, it is even scarce in online RL and not a common practice though. Moreover, to the best of our knowledge, the effect of increased batch sizes on ensembles is not documented in supervised learning as well. 

On the impact side, the use of ensembles for new offline RL methods becomes a popular choice to achieve competitive results [1, 2, 3]. And as far as we know, the main driving force for algorithmic improvements is to diversify the ensemble. On the opposite side, in our work, we demonstrated that it can be bypassed to some extent with the use of large batches with the benefits of achieving higher scores and faster convergence rates.

___
*References*

[1] Ghasemipour, S. K. S., Gu, S. S., & Nachum, O. (2022). Why So Pessimistic? Estimating Uncertainties for Offline RL through Ensembles, and Why Their Independence Matters. arXiv preprint arXiv:2205.13703.

[2] In Review at ICLR2023, “Lightweight Uncertainty for Offline Reinforcement Learning via Bayesian Posterior”, https://openreview.net/forum?id=55Eet8WGJTv

[3] Yang, R., Bai, C., Ma, X., Wang, Z., Zhang, C., & Han, L. (2022). RORL: Robust Offline Reinforcement Learning via Conservative Smoothing. arXiv preprint arXiv:2206.02829

content.comment:
> Diamond and white squares are not defined in figure 1.

Thank you, we updated the corresponding caption.

> The fact that results does't change that much by reducing the number of Qs in SAC-N from 500 to 50 tells that Qs are not that diverse. I believe that is what EDAC studies. Plotting means and standard deviation of Qs during training can help to better understand this.

Sorry, if we were not being clear enough in the paper, but the original SAC-N algorithm results in poor scores with 50 Qs (the original paper states the minimum number of critics to make it work, and it is 500). On the other hand, the proposed large batch utilization allows for achieving good scores even with 50 critics → the use of large batches allows to reduce the ensemble size. Moreover, in the updated version of the paper, we demonstrate that it works even with a lower number of critics (20 to 40 depending on the Hopper-v2 datasets).

content.title: Paper Decision
content.metareview:_summary,_strengths_and_weakn: This paper studies the batch size scaling of SAC-N, an offline RL algorithm, and finds that the practice of increasing the batch size while scaling the learning rate with the square root (common in other areas of ML) works well empirically. As various reviewers point out, the contribution is fairly incremental: similar empirical analyses are already commonplace, and the offline RL setting doesn't appear to raise any new considerations. This submission does not seem to meet the significance bar for ICLR.
